question: In 'The Tale of Melon City', why does the king order a noose to be set up to hang someone? 🪢
options: His crown was knocked off by an arch built too low 👑
The citizens refused to pay taxes 💰
answer: His crown was knocked off by an arch built too low 👑
explanation: Perfect! The 'just and placid' king felt terribly disgraced when the newly built arch knocked off his crown as he rode under it, so he foolishly ordered the builder to be hanged. 🏛️
hint: It involved a piece of royal headgear falling off.

question: How does the poet sarcastically describe the King at the beginning of the poem? 👑
answer: Just and placid 😇
explanation: Brilliant! Vikram Seth uses satire by describing the king as 'just and placid', even though his actions throughout the poem are completely foolish and impulsive. 🎭
hint: It means fair and calm, though the king acts the opposite.

question: What did the King order to be constructed over the public thoroughfare? 🏗️
answer: An arch 🌉
explanation: Spot on! The King ordered an arch to be built so that it would 'edify' the spectators and display his grand vision to the public. 🛣️
hint: It is a curved structure spanning an opening.

question: What reason did the King give for building the structure? 📜
answer: To edify the spectators 👁️
explanation: Excellent! The king wanted the structure to 'edify' or morally and intellectually improve the citizens who walked under it. 🏛️
hint: He wanted to uplift or enlighten the people looking at it.

question: Who was the first person the King blamed for the low arch? 👷
answer: The Chief of Builders 🏗️
explanation: Awesome! As soon as his crown fell, the furious King immediately blamed the Chief of Builders and ordered him to be hanged. 🪢
hint: He is the head person in charge of the construction crew.

question: Who did the Chief of Builders pass the blame onto? 🗣️
answer: The Workmen ⛏️
explanation: Fantastic! To save his own life, the Chief of Builders shifted the blame to the workmen who actually constructed the arch. 🏃
hint: They are the daily wage laborers who did the physical work.

question: How did the Workmen defend themselves from being hanged? 🛡️
options: They said they were on leave 🏖️
They said the bricks were made of the wrong size 🧱
answer: They said the bricks were made of the wrong size 🧱
explanation: Perfect! The workmen cleverly passed the buck by stating that the fault lay with the people who manufactured the bricks in the wrong size. 🏭
hint: They blamed the building materials used.

question: After hearing the workmen's defense, who did the King summon next? 🧱
answer: The Masons 👷
explanation: Brilliant! Since the bricks were the wrong size, the King logically (in his foolish way) called the Masons who were responsible for laying and sizing the bricks. 🏛️
hint: These are the professionals who work with stone and bricks.

question: Who did the Masons blame for the faulty arch? 📐
answer: The Architect 📏
explanation: Spot on! The Masons trembled with fear and quickly shifted the blame to the Architect who drew the original plans. 📜
hint: The person who designs buildings.

question: How did the Architect turn the blame back onto the King? 👑
options: He said the King gave him the wrong measurements 📏
He reminded the King that His Majesty had amended the original plans 📜
He said the King rushed the project ⏳
He claimed the King never paid him 💰
answer: He reminded the King that His Majesty had amended the original plans 📜
explanation: Excellent! The Architect cleverly reminded the King that he had presented the plans, and the King himself had made changes (amendments) to them. 🖋️
hint: He pointed out that the King made changes to the blueprints.

question: How did the King react when the Architect blamed him? 😲
options: He lost his head and got extremely confused 🤯
answer: He lost his head and got extremely confused 🤯
explanation: Awesome! Realizing he was the one at fault, the 'just and placid' King panicked, lost his composure, and didn't know what to do next. 😵
hint: He became very bewildered and stressed.

question: Who did the King call upon to solve the tricky situation of who to hang? 🧙‍♂️
options: The Wisest Man in the country 🧠
answer: The Wisest Man in the country 🧠
explanation: Fantastic! In his state of confusion, the King demanded some counsel and sent for the Wisest Man in the land to pass a verdict. 📜
hint: He sought advice from someone considered highly intelligent.

question: How was the 'Wisest Man' identified in this kingdom? 👴
options: By the number of books he read 📚
Simply by being the oldest man 🦯
answer: Simply by being the oldest man 🦯
explanation: Perfect! In this satirical poem, wisdom is foolishly equated merely with old age. The chosen man was so old he could neither walk nor see. 🧓
hint: Age was the only criteria used.

question: How was the Wisest Man brought to the Royal Court? 🛏️
options: He was carried there because he was so frail 🪑
He flew in on a carpet 🪄
answer: He was carried there because he was so frail 🪑
explanation: Brilliant! The poem highlights the absurdity of the situation by showing that the 'wisest' man was so old and weak he couldn't even walk and had to be carried. 🏥
hint: He was physically unable to use his legs.

question: Who did the Wisest Man declare as the real culprit that must be hanged? 🌉
answer: The Arch itself 🌉
explanation: Spot on! The frail old man gave an absurd verdict, stating that since the Arch was the thing that knocked off the crown, the Arch itself must be hanged! 🤦‍♂️
hint: He blamed an inanimate object.

question: Why couldn't they hang the Arch? 🛡️
options: It was too heavy to lift 🏋️
A councillor pointed out that it had touched the royal head, making it sacred 👑
answer: A councillor pointed out that it had touched the royal head, making it sacred 👑
explanation: Excellent! Just as the Arch was led to the scaffold, a councillor argued it would be a disgrace to hang something that had touched the King's head. 🤯
hint: It made physical contact with something royal.

question: How did the crowd react while the blame game was going on? 😠
options: They were cheering for the King 🎉
They became restless and started muttering 🌩️
answer: They became restless and started muttering 🌩️
explanation: Awesome! The public had gathered to watch a hanging. When nobody was being punished, they grew restless and demanded action, putting pressure on the King. 👥
hint: They were losing patience and getting angry.

question: What did the King decide when he saw the mood of the crowd? 🪢
options: He decided that *someone* must be hanged immediately to satisfy them ⚖️
He ordered the crowd to be arrested ⛓️
answer: He decided that *someone* must be hanged immediately to satisfy them ⚖️
explanation: Fantastic! Fearing a rebellion from the restless crowd, the foolish King decreed that the nation wanted a hanging, so *anyone* who fit the noose would hang. 🤦‍♀️
hint: He wanted to quench their thirst for a spectacle.

question: What was the bizarre method used to decide who would hang? 📏
options: Measuring everyone's height against the noose 🧍‍♂️
answer: Measuring everyone's height against the noose 🧍‍♂️
explanation: Perfect! The noose was set up at a specific height, and the royal decree stated that whoever was tall enough to fit the noose would be the one to hang. 📐
hint: It involved checking physical height.

question: Who was the only person in the kingdom tall enough to fit the noose perfectly? 👑
answer: The King himself 🧍
explanation: Brilliant! In a twist of dark irony, the King was the only man tall enough to fit the noose, leading to his own execution by his own command. 🪢
hint: The ruler of the land.

question: What happens to the King in the end of the blame game? 💀
options: He runs away to a forest 🌳
He is hanged by the Royal Decree 🪢
answer: He is hanged by the Royal Decree 🪢
explanation: Spot on! The King becomes a victim of his own absurd sense of justice and is hanged because he was the only one who fit the noose. ⚖️
hint: He faces the ultimate punishment he ordered.

question: How did the Ministers feel after the King was hanged? 😌
options: They were furious with the crowd 😡
They breathed a sigh of relief that they found someone to hang 😮‍💨
They decided to hang themselves too 🪢
answer: They breathed a sigh of relief that they found someone to hang 😮‍💨
explanation: Excellent! The ministers were practical and cynical; they were just relieved that the unruly crowd was satisfied, even if it meant the King died. 🏛️
hint: They were glad a crisis with the public was averted.

question: According to the kingdom's custom, how was the next King chosen? 🚪
options: The first person to pass the City Gate got to choose 🚶‍♂️
A royal parrot picked a name 🦜
answer: The first person to pass the City Gate got to choose 🚶‍♂️
explanation: Awesome! The ministers followed a bizarre custom where the next person to walk past the City Gate had the authority to name the new King. 🏰
hint: It depended on who walked through a specific entrance.

question: Who was the first person to pass the City Gate? 🤪
answer: An idiot 🤪
explanation: Fantastic! In keeping with the poem's satirical tone, the first person to pass the gate—and thus the one responsible for choosing the ruler—was an idiot. 🤦‍♂️
hint: Someone lacking intelligence.

question: When the guards asked the idiot who should be King, what did he answer? 🍈
answer: A melon 🍈
explanation: Perfect! The idiot replied 'A melon' because he loved melons. It was his standard answer to every question he was ever asked! 🍉
hint: It is a large, sweet fruit.

question: Why did the idiot choose a melon as the new king? 😋
options: Because he thought it looked like a crown 👑
Because it was his standard answer to all questions, as he liked melons 🍉
Because the melon spoke to him 🗣️
Because he was carrying a melon 🧺
answer: Because it was his standard answer to all questions, as he liked melons 🍉
explanation: Brilliant! The idiot lacked the mental capacity to understand the question. He just said 'A melon' because that was what he loved and always talked about. 🤪
hint: It was his favorite food.

question: What did the ministers do after the idiot named a melon? 👑
options: They laughed and waited for someone else 😂
They crowned a melon and placed it on the throne 🍈
They threw the idiot in jail ⛓️
answer: They crowned a melon and placed it on the throne 🍈
explanation: Spot on! Blindly following their absurd custom, the ministers literally took a melon, crowned it, and reverently placed it on the throne. 🏛️
hint: They took his answer completely literally.

question: What is the primary literary device used throughout 'The Tale of Melon City'? 🎭
answer: Satire/Irony 🙃
explanation: Excellent! Vikram Seth uses satire to mock blind adherence to rules, foolish leadership, and the absurdity of justice systems. 📖
hint: It uses humor, irony, and exaggeration to criticize foolishness.

question: How do the citizens feel about having a Melon for a King? 😌
options: They are happy and content because he doesn't interfere in their lives 🕊️
answer: They are happy and content because he doesn't interfere in their lives 🕊️
explanation: Awesome! The citizens are completely satisfied because a melon cannot make foolish laws or interfere in their daily business. They enjoy total freedom! 🌾
hint: They enjoy being left alone.

question: What economic/political philosophy is highlighted by the citizens' attitude toward the Melon King? 🕊️
answer: Laissez-faire (Non-interference) ⚖️
explanation: Fantastic! 'Laissez-faire' means letting things take their own course without interfering. The citizens love the Melon King because he lets them live in peace. 🍃
hint: A French term meaning 'let do' or non-interference.

question: What does the phrase 'custom is custom' imply in the context of the poem? 📜
options: People blindly follow rules without using logic or common sense 🙈
answer: People blindly follow rules without using logic or common sense 🙈
explanation: Perfect! The ministers defend crowning a melon by saying 'custom is custom', highlighting how foolish it is to follow traditions without questioning them. 🤦‍♂️
hint: It points to a lack of critical thinking.

question: Who is the author of the poem 'The Tale of Melon City'? ✍️
answer: Vikram Seth 🖋️
explanation: Brilliant! The poem was written by the acclaimed Indian author and poet Vikram Seth, known for his witty and narrative verse. 📚
hint: He also wrote 'A Suitable Boy'.

question: What does the king's crown falling off symbolize? 👑
options: Loss of authority, dignity, and a blow to his ego 📉
answer: Loss of authority, dignity, and a blow to his ego 📉
explanation: Spot on! The crown falling off represents a public humiliation and a loss of royal dignity, which triggers the king's absurd anger. 😤
hint: It represents a blow to his pride and power.

question: In the poem, what is the 'noose' a symbol of? 🪢
answer: Blind, irrational justice and punishment ⚖️
explanation: Excellent! The noose represents a broken justice system that cares more about punishing *someone* to satisfy the mob than finding the actual truth. 🏛️
hint: It represents an unfair system of penalty.

question: What was the Architect's tone when he spoke to the King? 🗣️
options: Calm and clever, shifting the blame 🧠
answer: Calm and clever, shifting the blame 🧠
explanation: Awesome! The Architect didn't panic; he cleverly and calmly pointed out that the King himself had amended the plans, neatly trapping the monarch. 🎯
hint: He was very smart about how he defended himself.

question: What ultimately caused the death of the King? 💀
answer: His own foolishness and vanity 🤦‍♂️
explanation: Fantastic! The King's death wasn't an accident; it was the direct result of his foolish decrees, his inability to make a sound decision, and his fear of the crowd. 🎭
hint: It was his own personality flaws.

question: Why did the King agree to let the crowd have a hanging? 👥
options: He wanted to test the noose 🪢
He was afraid the restless crowd would rebel against him 😨
answer: He was afraid the restless crowd would rebel against him 😨
explanation: Perfect! The king noticed the crowd muttering and becoming restless. Fearing a revolt, he foolishly decided to appease them with a hanging. ⚖️
hint: He was scared of public outrage.

question: What does the poem say about the 'public' or the crowd? 🌩️
options: They are fickle, bloodthirsty, and demand a spectacle 🩸
answer: They are fickle, bloodthirsty, and demand a spectacle 🩸
explanation: Brilliant! The poem satirizes the public as well, showing them as a mindless mob that doesn't care about justice, they just want the entertainment of a hanging. 🎪
hint: They just wanted to see a show of punishment.

question: How did the poet structure the rhymes in 'The Tale of Melon City'? 🎵
answer: Rhyming couplets (AABB) 🎭
explanation: Spot on! Vikram Seth wrote the poem in rhyming couplets, which gives it a musical, folklore-like rhythm that contrasts perfectly with the dark comedy of the story. 🎶
hint: Every two consecutive lines rhyme with each other.

question: What is the ultimate irony of the King's title 'just and placid'? 🙃
options: He is actually unjust, impulsive, and easily manipulated 🌪️
He is actually a brave warrior ⚔️
answer: He is actually unjust, impulsive, and easily manipulated 🌪️
explanation: Excellent! The irony is that a 'just and placid' king should be fair and calm. Instead, he orders executions over minor insults and panics under pressure. 👑
hint: His actions contradict the meaning of the words.

question: What did the 'Wisest Man' say in a 'quavering voice'? 🗣️
answer: Hang the Arch 🌉
explanation: Awesome! In his quavering, frail voice, the supposedly wise old man absurdly declared that the arch itself must be punished for knocking off the crown. 👴
hint: He blamed the stone structure.

question: When did this story take place according to the citizens? 🕰️
answer: Long, long ago ⏳
explanation: Fantastic! When asked about their Melon King, the citizens say this happened 'long ago', indicating that the story has become a piece of established folklore in their city. 📖
hint: It is framed as an ancient tale.

question: What was the King's reaction when the Architect said, 'You made certain amendments to the plans'? 📝
options: He turned pale and lost his head 😨
answer: He turned pale and lost his head 😨
explanation: Perfect! Hearing that the fault was entirely his own, the King's face went pale and he panicked, showing how weak and cowardly he truly was. 🥶
hint: He was terrified and confused.

question: What is the primary message the poet conveys through the Melon King? 🍈
options: A ruler who does nothing is often preferred over a foolish, active one 👑
answer: A ruler who does nothing is often preferred over a foolish, active one 👑
explanation: Brilliant! The poet suggests that people are perfectly happy with a figurehead (like a melon) who leaves them alone, rather than a human king whose foolishness disrupts their lives. 🕊️
hint: It's about the preference for non-interfering governance.

question: Why didn't the citizens mind that their King was a melon? 🤷‍♂️
options: They thought it was a magic melon ✨
They enjoyed peace and liberty under his non-interference 🕊️
They planned to eat him later 🍽️
answer: They enjoyed peace and liberty under his non-interference 🕊️
explanation: Spot on! The citizens state that as long as the King leaves them in 'Peace and Liberty', they don't care if he is a melon. They value their freedom above all. 🍃
hint: It allowed them to live without royal interruptions.

question: The process of measuring people's heights to fit a noose highlights which flaw in the kingdom? 📏
options: The complete lack of logic and blind pursuit of a scapegoat ⚖️
The advanced technology of the time ⚙️
answer: The complete lack of logic and blind pursuit of a scapegoat ⚖️
explanation: Excellent! The fact that they just wanted *any* neck to fit the noose, regardless of guilt, shows a completely broken and illogical justice system. 🤦‍♀️
hint: It shows they didn't care about real justice, just finding a victim.

question: What is the tone of the line 'The King was just and placid'? 🎭
answer: Sarcastic/Ironical 🙃
explanation: Awesome! Vikram Seth uses dramatic irony here. He sets up the King as 'just and placid' only to show him acting completely erratic and unfair in the very next stanzas. 📖
hint: He means the exact opposite of what the words say.

question: What role does the 'idiot' play in the poem's thematic structure? 🤪
options: He shows the absurdity of relying on blind customs to make important decisions 🎲
answer: He shows the absurdity of relying on blind customs to make important decisions 🎲
explanation: Fantastic! The custom of letting the first passerby choose the king is foolish. The fact that the passerby is an idiot who chooses a fruit highlights the utter absurdity of this tradition. 🍉
hint: He exposes how silly their rules are.

question: What do the ministers say when someone asks them why their King appears to be a melon? 🗣️
options: Custom is custom, and it's His Majesty's choice to be a melon 🍈
answer: Custom is custom, and it's His Majesty's choice to be a melon 🍈
explanation: Perfect! The citizens and ministers defend their strange reality by shrugging it off. They respect the custom that chose the melon and prefer the peace it brings. 📜
hint: They refer back to their traditions and accept it.

question: Overall, 'The Tale of Melon City' reads like a folktale. What makes it modern and thought-provoking? 🤔
options: Its sharp political satire on governance and justice 🏛️
answer: Its sharp political satire on governance and justice 🏛️
explanation: Brilliant! While it has the simple rhythm and style of a children's fable, its core is a sharp, biting critique of political systems, blind justice, and foolish leaders. 🌍
hint: It makes fun of how countries and laws are run.
